claim: Male Long-Evans rats were used in the study.
source: Male Long–Evans hooded adult rats (Charles Rivers Laboratories) with 3–5 months of age and weighing 300–450 g at the time of the experiment were used.
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section describing the animals used.

claim: Rats were food-restricted to 18 g of chow per day during the study.
source: Food-restricted rats (18 g of chow per day) were initially placed in an operant box and trained to press a lever for sucrose in the presence of audiovisual cues that signaled the availability of food.
evidence: Explicitly stated in the results section describing the behavioral paradigm.

claim: Rats exhibited increased freezing during olfactory threat conditioning training.
source: Rats showed robust defensive responses during the threat conditioning training, as evidenced by an increase in freezing (Shapiro–Wilk normality test, p < 0.001, Friedman test, Friedman statistic = 84.08, p < 0.001; Dunn's post hoc, p < 0.001) during the conditioned odor presentation (Figure 1B)
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data showing significant increase in freezing responses, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Rats showed a decrease in lever presses during threat conditioning training.
source: and a decrease in lever presses (Figure 1C, Shapiro–Wilk normality test, p < 0.001, Friedman test, Friedman statistic = 35.11, p < 0.001; Dunn's post hoc, p < 0.001)
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data showing significant decrease in lever pressing, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Rats showed increased latency to press the lever during threat conditioning training.
source: and an increase in the latency to press the lever (Figure 1D, Shapiro–Wilk normality test, p < 0.001, Friedman test, Friedman statistic = 29.45, p < 0.001; Dunn's post hoc, p < 0.001) during the presentation of the food cues across trials.
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data showing significant increase in latency to press, with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Two distinct behavioral phenotypes emerged during the conflict phase: Pressers and Non-pressers.
source: Interestingly, when we analyzed the percentage of rewarded presses during the conflict phase (Figure 1J), two behavioral phenotypes emerged: (1) rats that continued to press the lever for food in the presence of the threatening odor (Pressers, Figure 1K) and (2) rats that showed a complete suppression in lever presses in the presence of the threatening odor (Non-pressers, Figure 1L).
evidence: Direct observation and classification of behavioral responses during the conflict phase, with references to Figures 1J, 1K, and 1L.

claim: Pressers showed lower freezing responses than Non-pressers during the odor and conflict phases.
source: Pressers showed a lower percentage of time exhibiting freezing (Figure 1M, two-way repeated measures analysis of variance [ANOVA], interaction – F(2, 60) = 29.54, p < 0.001, Bonferroni post hoc test – odor phase, p < 0.001; conflict phase, p < 0.001)
evidence: Statistical comparison between Pressers and Non-pressers showing significant differences in freezing behavior, with reference to Figure 1M.

claim: Pressers showed lower avoidance responses than Non-pressers during the odor and conflict phases.
source: and avoidance responses (Figure 1N, two-way repeated measures ANOVA, interaction – F(2, 60) = 23.27, p < 0.001, Bonferroni post hoc test – odor phase, p < 0.001; conflict phase, p < 0.001)
evidence: Statistical comparison between Pressers and Non-pressers showing significant differences in avoidance behavior, with reference to Figure 1N.

claim: Pressers spent more time approaching the food area than Non-pressers during the odor and conflict phases.
source: and a greater percentage of time approaching the food area (Figure 1P, two-way repeated measures ANOVA, interaction – F(2, 60) = 22.49, p < 0.001, Bonferroni post hoc test – odor phase, p = 0.0453; conflict phase, p < 0.001) when compared to Non-pressers during both the odor and the conflict phases.
evidence: Statistical comparison between Pressers and Non-pressers showing significant differences in time spent in food area, with reference to Figure 1P.

claim: Pressers and Non-pressers showed similar lever pressing rates during cued food-seeking training.
source: Pressers and Non-pressers showed similar lever pressing rates during the cued food-seeking training (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B; two-way repeated measures ANOVA, interaction – F(1, 55) = 0.1065, p = 0.7454)
evidence: Statistical comparison showing no significant difference between groups during training, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Pressers and Non-pressers showed similar freezing levels during threat conditioning.
source: and threat conditioning phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; two-way repeated measures ANOVA, F(1, 51) = 0.265, p = 0.608), as well as the same freezing levels (two-way repeated measures ANOVA, F(1, 51) = 3.737, p = 0.058)
evidence: Statistical comparison showing no significant difference between groups during threat conditioning, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: PL neurons respond to both threat- and reward-associated cues.
source: Neurons in the prelimbic (PL) cortex respond to both threat- and reward-associated cues.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a known fact about PL neurons.

claim: Pressers showed a higher number of food-cue responsive neurons than Non-pressers during the reward phase.
source: When PL activity was time locked to the onset of the food cues during the reward phase, Pressers showed a higher number of food-cue responsive neurons than Non-pressers (Figure 2C, D vs. Figure 2M, N; Fisher Exact Test, 33% in Pressers vs. 21% in Non-pressers, p = 0.0418)
evidence: Statistical comparison of neural responses between Pressers and Non-pressers, with references to Figures 2C, D, M, N.

claim: Both Pressers and Non-pressers showed a reduction in food-cue responsive neurons from reward to conflict phase.
source: During the conflict phase, both Pressers and Non-pressers showed a significant reduction in the number of food-cue responsive neurons (Figure 2C, D vs. Figure 2M, N; Fisher Exact Test, from 33% to 14% in Pressers, p < 0.001; from 21% to 6% in Non-pressers, p = 0.0086)
evidence: Statistical analysis showing significant reduction in responsive neurons in both groups, with references to Figures 2C, D, M, N.

claim: Pressers displayed a higher proportion of sustained excitatory food-cue responses during the reward phase compared to Non-pressers.
source: We revealed that Pressers display a higher proportion of sustained excitatory responses during the reward phase, when compared to Non-pressers (Figure 2F vs. Figure 2P, 50% in Pressers vs. 10% in Non-pressers, Fisher Exact Test, p = 0.032).
evidence: Statistical comparison of sustained vs. transient responses between groups, with references to Figures 2F and 2P.

claim: Food-cue-evoked excitatory PL activity in Pressers was inversely correlated with lever press latency during the conflict phase.
source: A correlation analysis during the conflict phase revealed that food-cue-evoked excitatory PL activity in Pressers was inversely correlated with lever press latency, indicating that the higher the firing rate of food-cue responsive cells after the onset of the audiovisual cues, the quicker the animals searched for rewards (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Correlation analysis showing relationship between neural activity and behavior, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Different subsets of PL neurons signal freezing, avoidance, and risk-assessment behaviors.
source: We found that a small percentage of PL neurons changed their firing rates during the onset of freezing (Figure 3A), avoidance (Figure 3B), or risk-assessment (Figure 3C) behaviors in both Pressers and Non-pressers
evidence: Analysis of neural responses aligned to specific defensive behaviors, with references to Figures 3A, B, C.

claim: Most PL responsive neurons changed their activities exclusively during the onset of one defensive behavior.
source: Interestingly, most PL responsive neurons (80%) changed their activities exclusively during the onset of one of these three behaviors, with a reduced number of avoidance-responsive cells also responding during the onset of risk-assessment behavior (Figure 3J–M).
evidence: Analysis of neural response specificity across different behaviors, with references to Figures 3J-M.

claim: Pressers displayed increased power in the delta band compared to Non-pressers.
source: We therefore focused our analyses on these two bands and found that Pressers displayed increased power in the delta band, whereas Non-pressers exhibited increased power in the theta band during the three phases of the test session (Figure 4B, C, Welch's t-test of area under the curve, all p's < 0.001, see Source data 1).
evidence: Analysis of local field potential oscillations showing differences between groups, with references to Figures 4B, C.

claim: Non-pressers exhibited increased power in the theta band compared to Pressers.
source: We therefore focused our analyses on these two bands and found that Pressers displayed increased power in the delta band, whereas Non-pressers exhibited increased power in the theta band during the three phases of the test session (Figure 4B, C, Welch's t-test of area under the curve, all p's < 0.001, see Source data 1).
evidence: Analysis of local field potential oscillations showing differences between groups, with references to Figures 4B, C.

claim: The CaMKIIα promoter enables transgene expression favoring glutamatergic neurons in PL.
source: This CaMKIIα labeling approach has been successfully used in previous studies (Gradinaru et al., 2009; Tye et al., 2011) and was validated here for PL neurons by showing a lack of immunocolabeling between the viral vector and the GABAergic marker GAD67 (Figure 5A).
evidence: Validation of viral vector specificity through immunohistochemistry, with citation to previous studies and reference to Figure 5A.

claim: 36 out of 104 recorded PL neurons were classified as PLGLUT neurons based on photoidentification criteria.
source: Among the recorded PL cells, 36 out of 104 neurons (n = 5 rats) showed short-latency responses (<6 ms) and high spike reliability (Fano factor ratio >1) to laser illumination and were classified as PLGLUT neurons (Figure 5C, D and Materials and methods).
evidence: Quantification of photoidentified neurons based on specific electrophysiological criteria, with references to Figures 5C, D.

claim: The mDlx promoter enables transgene expression favoring GABAergic neurons in PL.
source: This mDlx labeling approach has been successfully used in previous studies (Dimidschstein et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2020), and was validated here for PL neurons by using two different methods: an immunohistochemical approach that resulted in significant immunocolabeling between the viral vector and the GABAergic marker GAD67 (Figure 5E), and an in situ hybridization approach which confirmed that ~88% of the cells labeled with the viral vector also expressed the GABAergic marker vGAT (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Validation of viral vector specificity through immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridization, with citations to previous studies and references to Figures 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: 69 out of 338 recorded PL neurons were classified as PLGABA neurons based on photoidentification criteria.
source: Among the recorded PL cells, 69 out of 338 neurons (n = 19 rats) showed short-latency responses (<6 ms) and high spike reliability (Fano factor ratio >1) to laser illumination and were classified as PLGABA neurons (Figure 5G, H and Materials and methods).
evidence: Quantification of photoidentified neurons based on specific electrophysiological criteria, with references to Figures 5G, H.

claim: PLGLUT neurons showed reduced spontaneous activity from the odor to the conflict phase in Pressers.
source: An average firing rate analysis across phases demonstrated that the activity of PLGLUT neurons did not change significantly from the reward to the odor phase (Fisher Exact Test, all p's > 0.05, see Source data 1), but was inhibited from the odor to the conflict phase when Pressers resumed searching for food (Figure 5O, Fisher Exact Test, odor vs. conflict, p = 0.0046).
evidence: Statistical analysis of spontaneous firing rates across phases in Pressers, with reference to Figure 5O.

claim: Photoactivation of PLGLUT neurons reduced lever press frequency during cued food seeking.
source: Photoactivation of PLGLUT (CaMKII-ChR2), but not PLGABA (mDlx-ChR2) neurons, reduced the frequency of lever presses (Figure 6M, two-way repeated measures ANOVA, F(10, 180) = 7.009, p < 0.001; Bonferroni post hoc, CaMKII-ChR2 vs. Control, all laser on periods – p < 0.001, mDlx-ChR2 vs. Control, all laser on periods – p > 0.05)
evidence: Optogenetic manipulation showing causal effect on behavior, with reference to Figure 6M.

claim: Photoactivation of PLGLUT neurons increased latency to press the lever during cued food seeking.
source: and increased the latency for the first press after the cue onset (Figure 6N, F(10, 180) = 9.931, p < 0.001; Bonferroni post hoc, CaMKII-ChR2 vs. Control, all laser on periods – p < 0.001, mDlx-ChR2 vs. Control, all laser on periods – p > 0.05), when compared to control group.
evidence: Optogenetic manipulation showing causal effect on behavior, with reference to Figure 6N.

claim: Photoactivation of PLGLUT or PLGABA neurons did not induce freezing behavior.
source: Photoactivation of either PLGLUT or PLGABA neurons did not induce freezing behavior (Figure 6O, F(10, 180) = 1.124, p = 0.346).
evidence: Optogenetic manipulation showing no effect on freezing, with reference to Figure 6O.

claim: Photoinhibition of PLGLUT neurons in Non-pressers reduced freezing responses during conflict.
source: Remarkably, photoinhibition of PLGLUT neurons (CaMKII-eNpHR, Shapiro–Wilk normality test, all p's < 0.05, see Source data 1) in Non-pressers reduced the percentage of time rats spent freezing (Figure 7D, Wilcoxon test, W = −64, laser off vs. laser on, p = 0.0020, Mann–Whitney test, U = 18 Control vs. CaMKII-eNpHR, p = 0.319)
evidence: Optogenetic manipulation showing causal effect on defensive behavior in Non-pressers, with reference to Figure 7D.

claim: Photoinhibition of PLGLUT neurons in Non-pressers reduced avoidance responses during conflict.
source: and avoiding the odor area (Figure 7E, Wilcoxon test, W = −21, laser off vs. laser on, p = 0.031; Mann–Whitney test, U = 19.5 Control vs. CaMKII-eNpHR, p = 0.365)
evidence: Optogenetic manipulation showing causal effect on defensive behavior in Non-pressers, with reference to Figure 7E.

claim: Photoinhibition of PLGLUT neurons in Non-pressers increased time spent in the food area during conflict.
source: and increased the percentage of time rats spent approaching the food area (Figure 7F, Wilcoxon test, W = 21, laser off vs. laser on, p = 0.031; Mann–Whitney test, U = 17 Control vs. CaMKII-eNpHR, p = 0.221) during the food-cue presentation, when compared to the eYFP-control group
evidence: Optogenetic manipulation showing causal effect on approach behavior in Non-pressers, with reference to Figure 7F.

claim: Photoinhibition of PLGLUT neurons in Non-pressers had no effect on lever pressing during conflict.
source: Despite the increase in food approaching behavior, photoinhibition of the same cells had no effect on the percentage of rewarded lever presses (Figure 7G, Wilcoxon test, W = 6, laser off vs. laser on, p = 0.250; Mann–Whitney test, U = 22.5 Control vs. CaMKII-eNpHR, p = 0.697)
evidence: Optogenetic manipulation showing no effect on lever pressing in Non-pressers, with reference to Figure 7G.

claim: Photoactivation of PLGABA neurons did not alter defensive or food-seeking behaviors during conflict.
source: In another subset of Non-pressers (Figure 7I–K), photoactivation of PLGABA neurons (mDlx-ChR2, Shapiro–Wilk normality test, all p's < 0.05, see Source data 1) did not alter freezing (Figure 7L, Wilcoxon test, W = 18, laser off vs. laser on, p = 0.156; Mann–Whitney test, U = 14 Control vs. mDlx-ChR2, p > 0.999), avoidance (Figure 7M, Wilcoxon test, W = 4, laser off vs. laser on, p = 0.500; Mann–Whitney test, U = 12 Control vs. mDlx-ChR2, p = 0.772) time in food area (Figure 7N, Wilcoxon test, W = −2, laser off vs. laser on, p = 0.750; Mann–Whitney test, U = 11 Control vs. mDlx-ChR2, p = 0.660) rewarded lever presses (Figure 7O, Wilcoxon test, W = 3, laser off vs. laser on, p = 0.500; Mann–Whitney test, U = 13.5 Control vs. mDlx-ChR2, p > 0.999) and latency to press the lever (Figure 7P, Wilcoxon test, W = −3, laser off vs. laser on, p = 0.500; Mann–Whitney test, U = 10 Control vs. mDlx-ChR2, p = 0.490)
evidence: Optogenetic manipulation showing no effect on behaviors in Non-pressers, with references to Figures 7L-P.

claim: PLGLUT neurons are necessary for the retrieval of conditioned threat responses.
source: Previous studies have shown that PL glutamatergic (PLGLUT) neurons are necessary for the retrieval of conditioned threat responses (Do-Monte et al., 2015)
evidence: Citation to previous study establishing role of PLGLUT neurons in threat memory retrieval.

claim: PLGABA neurons are implicated in both the encoding and retrieval of threat associations.
source: whereas PL GABAergic (PLGABA) neurons are implicated in both the encoding and the retrieval of threat associations by regulating the firing rate of PLGLUT neurons (Courtin et al., 2014; Cummings and Clem, 2019).
evidence: Citation to previous studies establishing role of PLGABA neurons in threat memory.

claim: The rodent mPFC is primarily composed of 75-85% excitatory glutamatergic cells.
source: The rodent mPFC, including PL, is primarily composed of excitatory glutamatergic cells that correspond to 75–85% of the neurons in this area.
evidence: Citation to previous studies establishing cellular composition of mPFC.

claim: Inhibitory GABAergic interneurons comprise 15-25% of neurons in the rodent mPFC.
source: In contrast, inhibitory GABAergic interneurons comprise 15–25% of the local neurons (Santana et al., 2004; Gabbott et al., 2005).
evidence: Citation to previous studies establishing cellular composition of mPFC.

claim: PL neurons are reciprocally connected with the basolateral nucleus of the amygdala.
source: PL neurons are reciprocally connected with the basolateral nucleus of the amygdala (BLA) (McDonald, 1991; Vertes, 2004), a region implicated in the detection of threats or rewards (Amir et al., 2015; Namburi et al., 2015; Beyeler et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: Citation to previous studies establishing anatomical connectivity and functional role of BLA.

claim: Increased activity in the BLA-PL pathway is sufficient and necessary for the expression of freezing responses.
source: In addition, during a modified Pavlovian cue discrimination task involving footshocks as punishment, increased activity in the BLA–PL pathway is sufficient and necessary for the expression of freezing responses (Burgos-Robles et al., 2017), a passive form of defensive behavior.
evidence: Citation to previous study establishing causal role of BLA-PL pathway in freezing.

claim: Inhibitory signaling in PL neurons correlates with threat-avoidance.
source: Conversely, inhibitory signaling in PL neurons correlates with threat-avoidance (Diehl et al., 2018), an active form of defensive behavior.
evidence: Citation to previous study showing correlation between PL inhibition and avoidance behavior.

claim: Increased delta power activity in the mPFC is associated with reward seeking and preparatory attention.
source: These findings are in corroboration with previous studies showing that increased delta power activity in the mPFC is associated with both reward seeking and preparatory attention (Horst and Laubach, 2013; Totah et al., 2013; Emmons et al., 2016)
evidence: Citation to previous studies establishing relationship between delta oscillations and reward-related behaviors.

claim: Augmented theta power in the mPFC is correlated with the expression of avoidance responses.
source: whereas augmented theta power in the mPFC or synchronized theta activity between mPFC and BLA is correlated with the expression of avoidance responses or the consolidation of threat memories, respectively (Popa et al., 2010; Padilla-Coreano et al., 2019).
evidence: Citation to previous studies establishing relationship between theta oscillations and defensive behaviors.

claim: 4 Hz LFP oscillations in the mPFC and BLA were strongly synchronized during conditioned freezing episodes.
source: In addition, prior studies have shown that 4 Hz LFP oscillations in the mPFC and BLA were strongly synchronized during conditioned freezing episodes (Courtin et al., 2014; Dejean et al., 2016; Karalis et al., 2016)
evidence: Citation to previous studies establishing synchronization of oscillations during freezing.

claim: Sustained 4 Hz oscillations in the mPFC were independent of hippocampal low-theta oscillations during freezing.
source: and these sustained 4 Hz oscillations in the mPFC were independent of hippocampal low-theta oscillations, suggesting that they were internally generated in the mPFC during the expression of freezing behavior (Karalis et al., 2016).
evidence: Citation to previous study establishing independence of mPFC oscillations from hippocampus.

claim: Inactivation of PLGLUT neurons may increase or reduce conditioned food-seeking responses depending on downstream projections.
source: In addition, during foraging in a safe context, food-associated cues activate both PLGLUT and PLGABA neurons (Burgos-Robles et al., 2013; Gaykema et al., 2014), and inactivation of PLGLUT neurons may increase or reduce conditioned food-seeking responses depending on the specific downstream projections that are being modulated (Otis et al., 2017).
evidence: Citation to previous studies establishing projection-specific effects of PLGLUT neurons on food seeking.

claim: Increased activity in mPFC neurons attenuates reward-seeking responses in a neutral context.
source: Our findings agree with previous studies showing that increased activity in mPFC neurons, including PL, attenuates reward-seeking responses in a neutral context (Berglind et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2013; Ferenczi et al., 2016; but see Warthen et al., 2016)
evidence: Citation to previous studies showing effect of mPFC activation on reward seeking.

claim: The effect of PL on reward seeking has been attributed to downstream projections to the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus.
source: an effect that has been attributed, at least in part, to downstream projections to the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (PVT) (Otis et al., 2017).
evidence: Citation to previous study identifying PVT as a downstream target mediating PL effects on reward seeking.

claim: PVT neurons are necessary for the retrieval of both reward- and threat-associated memories.
source: Notably, PVT neurons are necessary for the retrieval of both reward- and threat-associated memories (for a review see Do Monte et al., 2016; Millan et al., 2017; McGinty and Otis, 2020; Penzo and Gao, 2021)
evidence: Citation to review articles establishing role of PVT in memory retrieval.

claim: Activity in PVT neurons is associated with the regulation of approach-avoidance responses during conflict.
source: and activity in PVT neurons has recently been shown to be associated with the regulation of approach–avoidance responses during situations of conflict (Choi and McNally, 2017; Choi et al., 2019; Engelke et al., 2021)
evidence: Citation to recent studies showing role of PVT in conflict behavior.

claim: PL neurons are necessary to guide appropriate food-seeking behavior in tasks that rely on discrimination among environmental cues.
source: Collectively, these results add to a growing literature indicating that PL neurons are necessary to guide appropriate food-seeking behavior in tasks that rely on discrimination among environmental cues (Marquis et al., 2007; Sangha et al., 2014; Moorman and Aston-Jones, 2015)
evidence: Citation to previous studies establishing role of PL in cue discrimination during food seeking.

claim: Inactivation of PL neurons or their inputs from BLA increases risk-taking behavior in a conflict task.
source: Moreover, our results are in accordance with previous findings demonstrating that inactivation of PL neurons, or their inputs from BLA, increases risk-taking behavior in a conflict task in which rats needed to refrain from consuming sucrose to avoid a footshock (Burgos-Robles et al., 2017; Verharen et al., 2019).
evidence: Citation to previous studies showing effect of PL inactivation on risk-taking during conflict.

claim: PL neurons fire in response to shock-paired cues and such activity is correlated with freezing responses.
source: Previous studies have shown that PL neurons fire in response to shock-paired cues and such activity is highly correlated with the expression of freezing responses (Burgos-Robles et al., 2009; Sotres-Bayon et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2013; Courtin et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to previous studies establishing correlation between PL activity and freezing.

claim: Electrical stimulation or optogenetic induction of 4 Hz oscillations in PL increases conditioned freezing responses.
source: It also seems to disagree with previous studies showing that electrical stimulation or optogenetic induction of 4 Hz oscillations in PL increases conditioned freezing responses (Vidal-Gonzalez et al., 2006; Courtin et al., 2014) by synchronizing the neural activity between PL and BLA regions (Karalis et al., 2016).
evidence: Citation to previous studies showing effect of PL stimulation on freezing.

claim: Persistent avoidance of presumed threats is the cardinal symptom of anxiety disorders.
source: Whereas persistent avoidance of presumed threats is the cardinal symptom of anxiety disorders (Treanor and Barry, 2017)
evidence: Citation to previous study establishing clinical relevance to anxiety disorders.

claim: Seeking reward despite negative consequences is a hallmark of eating and substance use disorders.
source: seeking reward despite negative consequences is a hallmark of both eating and substance use disorders in humans (Volkow et al., 2012).
evidence: Citation to previous study establishing clinical relevance to addiction and eating disorders.

claim: The brain's ability to identify and discriminate cues associated with threat or reward allows organisms to respond appropriately to environmental changes.
source: The brain's ability to identify and discriminate cues associated with threat or reward allows organisms to respond appropriately to changes in the environment (Schultz, 2015; Hu, 2016).
evidence: Citation to previous studies establishing fundamental principle of cue-guided behavior.

claim: Animals respond to threatening cues with defensive behaviors including avoidance responses.
source: Animals respond to threatening cues with a series of defensive behaviors including avoidance responses that decrease their chances of being exposed to aversive outcomes (McNaughton and Corr, 2014; Krypotos et al., 2015; Cain, 2019).
evidence: Citation to previous studies establishing defensive behavioral responses to threats.

claim: Reward cues have attractive and motivational properties that elicit approach behavior.
source: In contrast, reward cues have attractive and motivational properties that elicit approach behavior (Robinson and Flagel, 2009; Morales and Berridge, 2020).
evidence: Citation to previous studies establishing approach behavior to reward cues.

claim: When animals are exposed to threat and reward cues simultaneously, an approach-avoidance conflict emerges.
source: When animals are exposed to threat and reward cues simultaneously, an approach–avoidance conflict emerges, and decision-making processes are recruited to resolve the situation (Kirlic et al., 2017; Barker et al., 2019).
evidence: Citation to previous studies establishing the concept of approach-avoidance conflict.

claim: Activity in PL neurons is necessary for the retrieval of both food- and threat-associated memories.
source: Accordingly, activity in PL neurons is necessary for the retrieval of both food- and threat-associated memories (Sierra-Mercado et al., 2010; Courtin et al., 2014; Sangha et al., 2014; Do-Monte et al., 2015; Otis et al., 2017).
evidence: Citation to previous studies establishing role of PL in memory retrieval.

claim: During a risky foraging task, dynamic modifications in PL and BLA activity correlate with detection of imminent threats and defensive readiness.
source: During a risky foraging task in rats, dynamic modifications in the activity of PL and BLA neurons correlate with the detection of imminent threats and the defensive readiness for action (Kim et al., 2018; Kyriazi et al., 2020).
evidence: Citation to previous studies showing correlation between PL/BLA activity and threat detection during foraging.

claim: Individual differences in risky decision-making have been reported in other rodent models of behavioral conflict.
source: Individual differences in risky decision-making have also been reported in other studies using rodent models of behavioral conflict involving footshock punishment (Simon et al., 2009; Jean-Richard-Dit-Bressel et al., 2019; Bravo-Rivera et al., 2021), reversal learning (Bari et al., 2010), or variations in reward probability (Ainslie, 1975; St Onge and Floresco, 2009; Dellu-Hagedorn et al., 2018)
evidence: Citation to previous studies showing individual variability in decision-making across different paradigms.

claim: Some neurobiological bases of individual variation in stimulus-reward response depend on differences in dopamine levels in subcortical circuits.
source: Evidence indicates that some of the neurobiological bases of individual variation in stimulus–reward response depend on differences in dopamine levels in subcortical circuits (Tomie et al., 2000; Flagel et al., 2007; Flagel et al., 2011), which are regulated by top-down mechanisms involving the mPFC (Ferenczi et al., 2016; Haight et al., 2017; Serrano-Barroso et al., 2019).
evidence: Citation to previous studies establishing role of dopamine and mPFC in individual variability.

claim: Reward-paired cues can acquire motivational salience in some subjects and become sufficient to elicit reward-seeking responses.
source: In support of this interpretation, reward-paired cues can acquire motivational salience in some subjects and become sufficient to elicit reward-seeking responses in both rodents (Robinson and Flagel, 2009; Robinson et al., 2014) and humans (Smith et al., 2011; Jensen and Walter, 2014).
evidence: Citation to previous studies showing motivational properties of reward cues across species.

claim: VTAGABA neurons correspond to 35% of cells in the ventral tegmental area and send projections to PL.
source: While the source of this inhibition is unclear, a potential candidate are GABAergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTAGABA), which correspond to 35% of the cells in this region and send significant projections to PL (Nair-Roberts et al., 2008; Breton et al., 2019).
evidence: Citation to previous studies establishing anatomy of VTAGABA neurons.

claim: VTAGABA neurons change their firing rates in response to reward-predicting cues.
source: Previous studies have shown that VTAGABA neurons change their firing rates in response to reward-predicting cues (Cohen et al., 2012)
evidence: Citation to previous study showing cue responses in VTAGABA neurons.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of VTAGABA neurons suppresses the activity of local dopaminergic neurons.
source: and chemogenetic activation of these cells suppress the activity of local dopaminergic neurons (van Zessen et al., 2012)
evidence: Citation to previous study showing effect of VTAGABA activation on dopamine neurons.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of VTAGABA neurons reduces cue-evoked sucrose-seeking responses.
source: reduces cue-evoked sucrose-seeking responses (Wakabayashi et al., 2019)
evidence: Citation to previous study showing effect of VTAGABA activation on reward seeking.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of VTAGABA neurons induces conditioned place aversion in rodents.
source: and induces conditioned place aversion in rodents (Tan et al., 2012).
evidence: Citation to previous study showing aversive effects of VTAGABA activation.

claim: Increased synchrony between mPFC and BLA activity in the theta frequency range has been reported for animals that successfully differentiate between aversive and safe cues.
source: More specifically, increased synchrony between mPFC and BLA activity in the theta frequency range has been reported for animals that successfully differentiate between aversive and safe cues (or environments) during a differential threat conditioning task (or an open field arena) (Likhtik et al., 2014; Stujenske et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to previous studies showing theta synchrony during cue discrimination.

claim: PL is comprised of different subpopulations of interneurons that inhibit each other during food seeking or defensive responses.
source: Because PL is comprised of different subpopulations of interneurons that inhibit each other during food seeking or defensive responses (Gaykema et al., 2014; Cummings and Clem, 2019), we cannot rule out the possibility that distinct subsets of PLGABA neurons were preferentially recruited during each one of the phases.
evidence: Citation to previous studies showing heterogeneity of PL interneurons.

claim: Reduced activity in PLGLUT neurons during conflict situations decreases defensive responses and biases behavior toward food seeking.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that reduced activity in PLGLUT neurons during conflict situations decreases defensive responses and biases rats' behavior toward food seeking.
evidence: Summary statement integrating optogenetic manipulation results.

claim: PLGLUT neurons establish a causal role in mediating individual variability in memory-based risky decision-making.
source: Our results establish a causal role for PLGLUT neurons in mediating individual variability in memory-based risky decision-making by regulating threat-avoidance vs. reward-approach behaviors.
evidence: Summary statement from abstract integrating all experimental findings.

claim: Under memory-based conflict situations, reduced or increased activity in PLGLUT neurons can favor the behavioral expression of food-approaching or threat-avoidance responses, respectively.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that under memory-based conflict situations, reduced or increased activity in PLGLUT neurons can favor the behavioral expression of food-approaching or threat-avoidance responses, respectively.
evidence: Summary statement integrating neural recording and optogenetic manipulation results.

claim: Differences in risk-taking and risk-avoiding behaviors were reflected in LFP frequencies in PL neurons from the beginning of the test session.
source: Differences in risk-taking and risk-avoiding behaviors were also reflected on LFP frequencies in PL neurons in the beginning of the test session, with Pressers and Non-pressers displaying increased power in the delta or theta bands, respectively.
evidence: Summary statement of LFP analysis results.

claim: Increased risk-taking behavior in Pressers was associated with a higher number of PLGLUT neurons showing reduced spontaneous activity during the conflict phase.
source: Increased risk-taking behavior in Pressers was associated with a higher number of PLGLUT neurons showing reduced spontaneous activity during the conflict phase.
evidence: Summary statement of photoidentification and recording results.

claim: Risk-avoiding responses in Non-pressers were associated with increased spontaneous activity in PL neurons during conflict.
source: In contrast, risk-avoiding responses in Non-pressers were associated with increased spontaneous activity during conflict.
evidence: Summary statement of photoidentification and recording results.

claim: Photoactivation of PLGLUT neurons is sufficient to recapitulate the reward-seeking suppression observed during conflict.
source: For instance, the reduction in food-seeking responses during photoactivation of PLGLUT neurons indicates that increased activity in PL pyramidal cells is sufficient to recapitulate the reward-seeking suppression observed during conflict.
evidence: Interpretation of optogenetic manipulation results.

claim: By reducing their spontaneous firing rates during conflict, PLGLUT neurons become more likely to fire in response to food cues due to an increase in signal-to-noise ratio.
source: In contrast, we speculate that by reducing their spontaneous firing rates during conflict situations, PLGLUT neurons become more likely to fire in response to food cues due to an increase in the signal-to-noise ratio, thereby resulting in persistent reward-seeking responses during the conflict phase as we propose in our schematic in Figure 8.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the mechanism by which reduced spontaneous activity enhances cue responses, with reference to Figure 8.

claim: Increased activity in the firing rate of PLGLUT neurons may result in reduced signal-to-noise ratio during food-cue onset.
source: Thus, it is possible that increased activity in the firing rate of PLGLUT neurons may result in reduced signal-to-noise ratio during the food-cue onset (Kroener et al., 2009; McGinley et al., 2015), and consequently decreased food-seeking responses.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of optogenetic activation results with citations to previous studies on signal-to-noise ratio.

claim: Other parallel brain regions may be modulating the suppression of operant lever-press responses during conflict.
source: The lack of effects on lever pressing indicates that other parallel brain regions may be modulating the suppression of operant lever-press responses during conflict.
evidence: Inference from the lack of effect of photoinhibition on lever pressing in Non-pressers.

claim: Photoinhibition of PLGLUT neurons was not large enough to produce a complete restoration of lever presses in Non-pressers.
source: Alternatively, photoinhibition of PLGLUT neurons was not large enough to produce a more global effect on risky behavior (i.e., completely restore lever presses).
evidence: Alternative interpretation for the lack of effect on lever pressing.

claim: The increased freezing responses following PL activation reported in previous studies appear to be dependent on the preexistence of a conditioned threat memory.
source: However, one important difference between our study and others is that photoactivation of PLGLUT neurons in our experiments was performed in naive rats, in the absence of shock-paired cues. Thus, the increased freezing responses following PL activation reported in previous studies appear to be dependent on the preexistence of a conditioned threat memory.
evidence: Inference from comparison of current results with previous studies to explain discrepancy.

claim: PL activity is indispensable to inhibit reward pursuit in the presence of threat-associated cues.
source: Additionally, our findings showing that inactivation of PLGLUT neurons increases food-approaching responses in Non-pressers suggest that PL activity is indispensable to inhibit reward pursuit in the presence of threat-associated cues.
evidence: Interpretation of photoinhibition results in Non-pressers.

claim: Differences in the number and magnitude of excitatory food-cue responses in PL neurons may contribute to individual differences in risky decision-making.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that differences in the number and magnitude of excitatory food-cue responses, as well as in the spontaneous activity of PL neurons during the conflict test, may contribute to the individual differences in risky decision-making observed between the two behavioral phenotypes.
evidence: Summary interpretation of neural recording results linking neural activity to behavioral phenotypes.

claim: PL neurons exhibit a heterogeneous pattern of activity during reward-seeking behavior.
source: These observations suggest that PL neurons exhibit a heterogeneous pattern of activity during reward-seeking behavior, consistent with a recent study using calcium imaging recordings from PL neurons in head-fixed mice (Grant et al., 2021).
evidence: Interpretation of neural recording results showing diverse response patterns, with citation to supporting study.

claim: Different subsets of PL neurons signal distinct behavioral outcomes during a conflict situation.
source: Overall, these results suggest that different subsets of PL neurons signal distinct behavioral outcomes during a conflict situation, with only a reduced number of PL neurons encoding the aversive salience of environmental cues independently of the defensive response expressed by the animal.
evidence: Summary interpretation of neural responses to different defensive behaviors.

claim: Distinct patterns of PL activity are associated with risk-taking or risk-avoiding behaviors in conflict situations.
source: While this set of results suggest that distinct patterns of PL activity are associated with risk-taking or risk-avoiding behaviors in conflict situations, our optogenetic manipulation provided a causal role for PLGLUT neurons in the regulation of approach–avoidance conflict.
evidence: Summary statement linking correlational and causal findings.

claim: PL neurons can distinguish between reward and conflict situations.
source: suggesting that PL neurons can distinguish between reward and conflict situations (Figure 2G vs. Figure 2H and Figure 2Q vs. Figure 2R).
evidence: Inference from the observation that neural responses differ between reward and conflict phases, with references to Figures 2G, H, Q, R.

claim: Distinct subpopulations of PLGLUT neurons encode reward- and threat-related information differently.
source: We found that all PLGLUT neurons that were either excited or inhibited during the reward phase responded in opposite direction or did not change their activities during the odor phase (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-B), suggesting the existence of distinct subpopulations of PLGLUT neurons that encode reward- and threat-related information differently in our task.
evidence: Inference from longitudinal tracking of neural activity across phases, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: Both glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons in PL may contribute to the expression of distinct defensive responses during conflict.
source: These results indicate that both glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons in PL may contribute to the expression of distinct defensive responses during conflict.
evidence: Inference from the observation that both cell types show responses to defensive behaviors.

claim: A significant proportion of PLGLUT neurons are inhibited when rat's behavior transitions from increased defensive responses to increased food-seeking responses.
source: Together, our data suggest that a significant proportion of PLGLUT neurons are inhibited when rat's behavior transitions from increased defensive responses during the conditioned odor phase to increased food-seeking responses during the conflict phase.
evidence: Summary interpretation of photoidentification and recording results across phases.

claim: The two behavioral phenotypes most likely emerged during the test session and were independent of prior differences in sucrose preference or food-seeking motivation.
source: During our approach–avoidance conflict test, Pressers and Non-pressers showed similar levels of lever pressing before the conflict phase (e.g., cued food-seeking training, threat conditioning, and reward phases). This observation suggests that these two individual phenotypes most likely emerged during the test session and were independent of prior differences in sucrose preference or food-seeking motivation.
evidence: Inference from the observation that groups showed similar behavior before the conflict phase.

claim: The increased defensive behaviors and reduced food-seeking responses in Non-pressers were unlikely due to higher acquisition of conditioned threat responses.
source: Similarly, because both groups exhibited the same percentage of freezing to the shock-paired odor during the olfactory threat conditioning session, the increased defensive behaviors and the reduced food-seeking responses observed in Non-pressers during the test session were unlikely due to higher acquisition of conditioned threat responses.
evidence: Inference from the observation that groups showed similar freezing during conditioning.

claim: Internal factors such as shock sensitivity or pain tolerance cannot account for the individual differences observed in the experiments.
source: Furthermore, other internal factors such as shock sensitivity or pain tolerance cannot be accounted for the individual differences observed in our experiments because both groups reacted equally to the unconditioned stimulus (i.e., velocity measured as maximum speed after the footshocks)
evidence: Inference from the observation that groups showed similar reactions to footshock.

claim: Pressers and Non-pressers have allocated distinct motivational significance to the food- or shock-paired cues during the test session.
source: Therefore, the most plausible interpretation for the behavioral differences observed in our task is that Pressers and Non-pressers have allocated distinct motivational significance to the food- or shock-paired cues during the test session.
evidence: Inference from ruling out alternative explanations for behavioral differences.

claim: The increase in the number and magnitude of food-cue responses in Pressers might result in a greater allocation of attention to reward cues.
source: Because PL neurons are known for encoding the value of reward-predictive cues (Sharpe and Killcross, 2015; Otis et al., 2017), the increase in the number and magnitude of food-cue responses observed in Pressers might result in a greater allocation of attention to reward cues, which would explain the persistent reward-seeking responses observed in this group during motivational conflict.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of neural recording results with citations to previous studies on PL function.

claim: The reduced excitatory food-cue responses in Non-pressers may be mediated by cue-evoked activity in inhibitory inputs to PL during the conflict phase.
source: Another possible interpretation for the differences in food-cue responses in Pressers and Non-pressers is the reduced excitatory food-cue responses in Non-pressers, which may be mediated by cue-evoked activity in inhibitory inputs to PL during the conflict phase.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of neural recording results.

claim: VTAGABA neurons are a potential source of inhibition to PL during conflict.
source: While the source of this inhibition is unclear, a potential candidate are GABAergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTAGABA), which correspond to 35% of the cells in this region and send significant projections to PL (Nair-Roberts et al., 2008; Breton et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculation about potential circuit mechanism with citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The regulation of rewarding and aversive responses by VTAGABA neurons can potentially be attributed to their long-range inhibitory projections to PL neurons during conflict situations.
source: Future studies need to determine whether this regulation of rewarding and aversive responses by VTAGABA neurons can also be attributed to their long-range inhibitory projections to PL neurons, particularly during conflict situations.
evidence: Speculation about future research directions based on current findings and previous literature.

claim: Non-pressers showed increased theta activity and marked 4 Hz oscillations in PL neurons, which were associated with better discrimination between reward and threat cues.
source: Consistent with these findings, in our study Non-pressers showed increased theta activity and marked 4 Hz oscillations in PL neurons, which were associated with better discrimination between reward and threat cues and increased freezing responses during the test session, when compared to Pressers.
evidence: Integration of LFP findings with behavioral observations.

claim: PVT is a potential target by which PL glutamatergic neurons may exert their effects on approach-avoidance conflict.
source: suggesting a potential target by which PL glutamatergic neurons may exert their effects.
evidence: Speculation about circuit mechanism based on previous literature on PL-PVT pathway.

claim: Elucidating mechanisms that mediate risk-taking vs. risk-avoiding responses may have clinical relevance to psychiatric disorders.
source: Elucidating the underlying mechanisms that mediate risk-taking vs. risk-avoiding responses during situations of uncertainty may help to provide understanding of response selection and adaptive behaviors, and may have clinical relevance to many psychiatric disorders (Aupperle and Paulus, 2010; Kirlic et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement of clinical relevance with citations to previous studies.

claim: All experimental procedures were approved by the Center for Laboratory Animal Medicine and Care of The University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston.
source: All experimental procedures were approved by the Center for Laboratory Animal Medicine and Care of The University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston.
evidence: Statement of ethical approval in methods section.

claim: The National Institutes of Health guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals were strictly followed.
source: The National Institutes of Health guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals were strictly followed to minimize any potential discomfort and suffering of the animals.
evidence: Statement of adherence to ethical guidelines in methods section.
